title: Numerical estimation of the capture ability of Neptunian mean motion resonances II. Influence of eccentricity and inclination
summary: Evaluating the ability of Neptunian mean-motion resonances (MMRs) to capture small bodies is an important step in reconstructing the evolutionary history of the early Solar System. Building on a previous planar model, this study extends the investigation of MMR capture during Neptune's migration to the three-dimensional case, systematically analyzing the effects of the small objects' eccentricity, e, and inclination, i. Through numerical simulations with different migration rates, we obtain the distribution of capture probabilities for 12 MMRs on the e-i plane. The results show that increasing i narrows the ``inevitable capture zone'' (strong MMRs and/or slow migration) and raises the lower e threshold for capture (weak MMRs and/or fast migration), while it may also expand the upper e limit for capture. When the resonance order reaches three, the e-i plane further differentiates into several regions, which are closely related to the types of resonant angles. The emerging i-dominated region, along with its inevitable capture zone, makes third-order MMRs the most likely to benefit from higher inclination, as well as the most likely to host mixed-type resonators. Finally, using a hypothetical planetesimal distribution, we calculated the capture probability and efficiency for each MMR, finding that a cold disk favors strong MMRs, whereas a hot disk reduces differences among MMRs and across migration rates. In the future, a better determination of the population associated with different MMRs and different types of objects will help us understand the dynamical excitation state of the primordial disk in the early Solar System.

title: Robustness of C/O and mean molecular weight under disequilibrium chemistry
summary: Transmission spectroscopy increasingly reduces exoplanet spectra to derived compositional metrics, such as C/O, O/H, and mean molecular weight (MMW), but these quantities do not carry molecular abundance uncertainties in the same way. We assessed the reliability of these metrics for hot Jupiters and sub-Neptunes, by combining analytic uncertainty propagation with photochemical VULCAN forward models and representative published retrieval constraints. Propagating molecular abundance uncertainties produced substantially larger fractional uncertainties in elemental abundance ratios than in MMW. The fractional uncertainties in C/O and O/H were typically comparable to the inferred ratios, whereas the fractional uncertainty in MMW was more than two orders of magnitude smaller in H2/He-dominated atmospheres. Photochemistry and vertical mixing redistributed individual molecules but produced only minor changes in C/O and MMW at the pressures probed by transmission spectroscopy. C/O remains an important diagnostic of atmospheric chemistry and planetary formation history, but its interpretation requires careful uncertainty propagation. Mean molecular weight may provide a comparatively stable population-level diagnostic for linking observable atmospheres to bulk composition, especially across the sub-Neptune radius valley.

title: Mid-infrared Imaging of SR 12 c with JWST/MIRI: Grain Growth in an Evolved Circumplanetary Disk
summary: The physical properties of circumplanetary disks offer insights into the formation of giant planets and their satellites. The circumbinary planetary-mass companion SR 12 c (1200 au from SR 12 AB) hosts an isolated dust disk directly detected with ALMA. We present JWST/MIRI imaging of SR 12 c from 5.6 to 21 $μ$m and analyze its spectral energy distribution from infrared to submillimeter wavelengths. Phenomenologically, the dust disk can be described by a two-component blackbody with large contrasts in characteristic temperatures and radii. Physically motivated models with varied geometries and heating mechanisms suggest a predominantly flat, irradiation-heated disk with a smaller contribution from viscous dissipation. The disk is inferred to be compact, with an inner radius of ~3 $R_{\rm Jup}$. The outer radius is only loosely constrained, with a characteristic value of ~3 au. The lack of strong 10 $μ$m excess emission suggests significant grain growth and dust settling. We also find that SR 12 c is broadly consistent with the empirical star-disk scaling relations, providing context for its possible formation pathway. These results demonstrate the power of combining mid-infrared and submillimeter observations with disk modeling to better understand the physical properties of circumplanetary disks.

title: Single-Transit Parameter Estimation with Calibrated Uncertainties
summary: The growing volume of photometric data from current and upcoming exoplanet surveys demands automated analysis pipelines to detect and characterize exoplanet transit signals. Among these, single-transit events present a challenge, since only one event is observed, and standard transit-fitting techniques for periodic signals do not directly apply because they rely on phase-folding. Beyond detection, characterizing these events is equally critical for follow-up, yet existing approaches are either sensitive to stellar variability and require prior detrending, or depend on stellar priors and per-target fitting. This work presents a convolutional neural network that predicts transit depth, duration, and mid-transit time, together with calibrated uncertainties, directly from a single transit signal. Our network is trained on synthetic light curves and evaluated against a trapezoidal least-squares baseline. On 120 confirmed exoplanets, both methods achieve comparable median errors, but the baseline fails to locate the transit in 10% of cases, producing unreliable estimates that would propagate into follow-up prioritization. In contrast, our network fails in only 1% of cases, yields lower mean absolute errors, and does not require detrending or stellar priors. Detrending would distort or remove the transit along with high stellar variability, precisely where the baseline fails and our network succeeds. Finally, we identify 169 new transit candidates in TESS Sectors 27-60 and apply our approach to obtain their physical parameters, creating a catalog that includes single-transit, multi-transit and multi-planet systems. This approach offers a scalable path toward automated characterization of single transit events, a population that will grow with upcoming surveys.

title: Spectroscopic Studies of Meteors within the Skytinel Network
comment: Submitted to Astronomische Nachrichten, 12 pages, 6 figures
summary: We present 12 low-resolution meteor spectra recorded at four stations of the Skytinel network in Poland, focusing on consistent reduction and comparison of Fe, Mg, and Na emission features. Spectra spanning approximately 350--850 nm were extracted, background-subtracted, and wavelength-calibrated using IRAF. Corrections accounted for the wavelength-dependent quantum efficiencies of Sony IMX249 and IMX273 detectors and atmospheric attenuation as a function of observing geometry. The corrected spectra were decomposed into Fe, Mg, and Na components using selected atomic transitions, temperature-dependent emissivities, and pseudo-Voigt line profiles. Integrated Fe~I-15, Mg~I-2, and Na~I-1 intensities were compared in a ternary diagram. Most spectra overlap with or lie near the normal-meteor distribution in reference samples, while some extend toward Fe-rich or Na-rich regions. The most Fe-dominated event assigns approximately 81\% of the summed emission to Fe~I-15. These ratios characterize relative emission, not elemental abundances or bulk composition. Combined with trajectory and photometric data, spectral classification may help constrain plausible material properties in dark-flight models and refine predicted meteorite search areas.

title: Companions of Hot Jupiters: two decades of radial velocity monitoring with CORALIE
comment: 17 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: Hot Jupiters are thought to form through multiple pathways, some of which can leave observable signatures in the architecture of their planetary systems. Massive outer companions, in particular, can provide important constraints on the dynamical histories of hot Jupiters. We aim to characterize the occurrence rate and orbital properties of additional giant companions in hot Jupiter systems, and to investigate whether these companions provide evidence for the role of dynamical interactions in shaping the hot Jupiter population. We perform a homogeneous long-term radial-velocity analysis of 147 WASP hot Jupiter systems observed with the CORALIE spectrograph between 2007 and 2025. We identify or refine 13 outer giant companions and use individual radial-velocity posteriors within a Bayesian occurrence-rate framework to measure the frequency of giant companions over orbital periods of 10--6250 days. The occurrence rate of additional giant companions increases strongly with orbital period, from {2}lt;0.01$ and 0.02 at 10--50 and 50--250 days to 0.05 and 0.17 at 250--1250 and 1250--6250 days, respectively, in agreement with the giant-planet occurrence of the general FGK population and with previous estimates of outer companions to hot Jupiters. Hot Jupiters with detected companions have longer orbital periods and higher eccentricities than those without. We also find that companion eccentricity decreases with hot Jupiter period, and that the companion-to-hot-Jupiter mass ratio increases with period ratio, both consistent with expectations from high-eccentricity migration (HEM). Our results support HEM as the mechanism shaping hot Jupiters with outer companions. Combining long-baseline radial velocities with future Gaia astrometry will further constrain companion masses, mutual inclinations, and dynamical histories.

title: Dynamical response of a protoplanetary disk to an FU Ori-type outburst
comment: Accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Episodic accretion events onto young stars can significantly change the global structure of their surrounding protoplanetary disks. Using radiation hydrodynamical simulations with the HURAKAN code, we study the response of the outer passive disk to a powerful FU Ori-type outburst. Disk heating initiates a factor-of-two increase in the vertical scale-height, which develops on a local keplerian timescale. This effectively launches an outward travelling wave with a bump whose radial position changes with time as $r_{b}\sim t^{2/3}$. After the outburst ends, new waves are launched as the disk structure re-equilibrates toward a quiescent state. The vertical expansion of the disk introduces significant time-variable extinction of the central source emission. Disks with inclinations in the range $40^{\circ}<i<60^{\circ}$ go from weakly ($A_{V}<1$) to a strongly embedded state ($A_{V}\sim10^2$), with the extinction decaying on a $\sim10^2$ yr timescale after the outburst. A fingerprint of the outburst-launched shadowing wave is a long-lived drop or a transient dip in the luminosity curve occurring several years after the outburst begins. This apparent luminosity variation is relatively large, up to $1^m-3^m$ in the V band, and is not related to the intrinsic accretion variability.

title: A 36.34-day Sub-Neptune Candidate Transiting the Nearby K Dwarf TIC 402710280
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Data and code: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23390273. Pre-registered test of the 2027 transits: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23390325
summary: We report a transiting sub-Neptune candidate with a period of 36.34 days around TIC 402710280 (TYC 9041-03677-1), a K dwarf of TESS magnitude 9.24 at 66.8 pc that the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) has observed only in full-frame images. Four transits, recorded between 2021 and 2026 in Sectors 39, 93, 100 and 102 and reduced by three independent pipelines, share a depth of $2092 \pm 47$ ppm and a duration of $5.27 \pm 0.05$ h. Two of them fall on consecutive cycles, and every shorter period predicts transits in covered data that are absent at $\geq 18.6σ$; the period is $P = 36.33986 \pm 0.00051$ d. A transit model gives $R_p/R_\star = 0.0421^{+0.0007}_{-0.0005}$ and a stellar density consistent with the host's. The candidate has a radius of $3.75 \pm 0.22 R_\oplus$ and an equilibrium temperature of $498 \pm 21$ K. Difference-image centroids place the signal $1.5'' \pm 1.3''$ from the target. The only catalogued star close enough to contribute, a background star $3.5''$ away, would have to host an eclipsing binary whose eclipse shape is disfavoured for any main-sequence pair ($Δχ^2 \geq 142$). No secondary eclipse is detected, and TRICERATOPS gives a false-positive probability of $0.003 \pm 0.004$. No high-resolution imaging exists, so companions within about $1''$ are constrained only by Gaia astrometry. The mid-times scatter about a linear ephemeris by 21.8 min (rms). Quick-Look Pipeline light curves reproduce the 29-min excess in the interval between the two 2026 transits, so it does not arise in our photometry; we report the scatter without choosing between an instrumental and a dynamical origin. The light curve also contains a $407 \pm 26$ ppm signal with a period of 3.78 days whose source, the target or the background star, the present data cannot identify. We predict transit times, including one in TESS Sector 114 on 2027 February 19.

title: The EMA Justitia Probe: Terminator Frame-Based Deployment Orbit Selection and Surface Coverage Analysis
comment: Accepted for publication in Acta Astronautica (Elsevier), 2026. This version is the author's accepted manuscript
summary: The Emirates Mission to the Asteroid Belt (EMA) probe is designed to perform asteroid imaging during an uncontrolled ballistic descent to (269) Justitia. The mission design is constrained by main spacecraft proximity operations, uncertain asteroid gravity, limited knowledge of the final deployment trajectory, and requirements for illumination and safe operations. These constraints necessitate a mission design that ensures suitable illumination, attitude determination and control, and payload pointing throughout descent. The EMA probe concept of operations employs near-terminator deployment orbit geometry with continuous Sun visibility and two attitude control modes: single-axis Sun-spin for periodic imaging opportunities and three-axis asteroid-pointing for continuous asteroid visibility. Based on these modes, formal requirements are derived for deployment orbits that enable asteroid observations during ballistic descent. A deployment orbit selection method is developed using the terminator reference frame and a minimum boresight deviation margin. The method identifies families of orbit orientations satisfying illumination and payload observation constraints. Reference orbits are selected and verified through mission geometry analysis and trajectory propagation using a polyhedron gravity model. Asteroid surface coverage is then evaluated for uncontrolled tumbling, Sun-spin, and asteroid-pointing modes. The results characterize the expected imaging performance and demonstrate the feasibility of the EMA probe concept for close-proximity asteroid imaging. The proposed approach can also support future ballistic probe missions subject to similar operational and observational constraints.
